findings.reason: The protected Python solution implements a FileSharing system using dual sparse mappings: user_chunks (user ID -> set of owned chunk IDs) and chunk_users (chunk ID -> set of user IDs). Reusable user IDs are managed using a min-heap (available_ids) and next_id counter. Operation methods join, leave, and request run in O(k + log U), O(k + log U), and O(p log p) time respectively, with O(U + H) auxiliary space. The implementation is expert quality; no candidate is required.

Popping from the min-heap available_ids guarantees the smallest unused positive integer user ID is assigned upon joining. Dual set updates maintain bidirectional consistency across join, leave, and request calls.

Join and leave update k ownership links and pop/push from min-heap in O(k + log U) time. Request sorts p current owners in O(p log p) time. Space complexity is O(U + H) for active user IDs and ownership pairs. Complexity evidence is inherited and hash-bound.
Accepts m chunks, supports join, leave, and request calls with correct return types and ID recycling.

The approach accurately details bidirectional set tracking, min-heap ID recycling, idempotent transfer rules, and O(k + log U) / O(p log p) time and O(U + H) space bounds. Alternatives and edge cases cover linear ID searches, monotone counter pitfalls, single-direction maps, pre-sorted list overhead, empty initial holdings, unavailable chunks, repeated requests, leaving after transfers, and multiple released IDs.

App Python and native Python solutions both execute the identical dual-map min-heap file sharing system design with SHA-256 digests ce52a33da9142701d9c45a64ac0e3666cb2e2ba20be361296023bd5a895446e2 and bce92479478af1a8ababbfd4a43948325d5fb00263a5469534ced7342aa3cde9.
